value.option_title: Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability
value.question: Does increasing the capacity of a neural ingredient-substitution model measurably improve its ranking of sustainable replacements, measured as Hit@1 on Recipe1MSubs [src_gismo_sizes]?
value.hypothesis: More capacity in a substitution ranker improves substitution ranking because larger encoders capture finer ingredient context, as LLM results suggest [src_llm].
held_fixed: Recipe1MSubs benchmark and its 10,747-sample test split
Contrastive loss, Adam optimizer, early stopping on validation MRR
5 seeds per width, ranking over the full vocabulary, MRR and Hit@k metrics

predictions.if_lever: Hit@1 rises with width, reaching at least 22 percent at width 512, above GISMo's 20.56, and still climbing.
predictions.if_not: Hit@1 plateaus near GISMo's 20.56 at every width; extra capacity adds nothing, so wider models are not the lever.
predictions.decision_rule: Compute is the lever if Hit@1 at width 512 minus Hit@1 at width 64 is at least 2.0 points and exceeds twice the pooled standard error; otherwise it is not.
predictions.noise_rule: Five seeds per width, mean and standard deviation reported; a real effect must exceed twice the pooled standard deviation, and GISMo's reported Hit@1 spread is 0.14 points.
predictions.expected_why: Published LLM fine-tuning lifted Hit@1 on this benchmark family from 34.53 to 38.03, so larger encoders should lift it here too [src_llm].

value.compute_tested_why: The test varies the ranker's embedding width, which sets model size and per-step FLOPs; wider models need more GPU memory and compute, so more GPUs buy the larger widths.
value.scored_against: Measured Hit@1 and MRR at each width are compared with GISMo's published 20.56 and 31.51 and the LT+Freq baseline's 18.10 and 27.66; a correct setup reproduces them within tolerance first.

arms.what: GISMo-style GIN ranker trained at embedding widths 64, 128, 256, 512 (the compute axis)
Optional stretch: a small pretrained transformer encoder with the GISMo scoring head, if the width sweep plateaus

baseline.what: LT+Freq statistical baseline (strongest non-neural): test MRR 27.66, Hit@1 18.10

anchor.what: Reproduce GISMo's published test-set MRR of 31.51 and Hit@1 of 20.56 using the official code, within 2 MRR points [src_gismo_gismo].
anchor.tolerance: plus or minus 2.0 MRR points (mean over 5 seeds)

checks: Downloaded splits contain 49,044 / 10,729 / 10,747 samples as published.
Ranking is over the 6,653-ingredient vocabulary, matching GISMo.
Anchor mean MRR lands within 2 points of 31.51 before the sweep starts.
Per-width results averaged over 5 seeds; a real gap exceeds twice the pooled standard deviation.
Best width re-evaluated on the high-footprint source-ingredient subset.

phases.what: Download Recipe1MSubs, FlavorGraph, and the gismo code; verify split counts; build the high-footprint ingredient list.
phases.stop_rule: Stop if the test split does not contain 10,747 samples.

phases.what: Reproduce GISMo: 5 training runs on one A100, timed.
phases.stop_rule: Stop after 5 runs or 12 GPU-hours, whichever comes first.

gate.else: halve the sweep to widths 64 and 128 with 3 seeds each and re-check the budget

phases.what: Train the ranker at widths 64, 128, 256, 512 with 5 seeds each (20 runs) on 4 A100s; measure Hit@1 and MRR.
phases.stop_rule: Stop after 20 runs or 10 wall-clock hours.

phases.what: Evaluate the best width on test tuples whose source ingredient is high-footprint (butter, egg, milk, cream, beef, pork, chicken, cheese, oil).
Optional: fine-tune a small pretrained transformer encoder with the GISMo scoring head, if the width sweep plateaus.

restructuring.sequential_part: Each training run waits on its own gradient epochs, roughly 30 per run; the runs themselves are independent.

scope_gap: The benchmark is home cooking, not industrial formulations; a real replacement needs a lifecycle footprint model and sensory validation, which this test does not buy.
Correct substitution ranking is not the same as a sustainable replacement; the test never measures emissions or production cost.

novelty.closest_prior: Rita 2024 fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and TinyLlama on Recipe1MSubs, lifting Hit@1 from 34.53 to 38.03; no capacity sweep within one protocol exists [src_llm].
novelty.left_open: Whether ranking quality keeps rising with model capacity inside one fixed protocol on Recipe1MSubs is unmeasured; the only scaling evidence is cross-protocol.

limits: Shows ranking accuracy on home recipes, not industrial formulations, and never measures actual environmental footprint or sensory quality of the substitute.
value.test_summary: Reproduce GISMo's Recipe1MSubs result, then train the ranker at four widths 64, 128, 256, 512 with five seeds each on four GPUs; if Hit@1 climbs past the 20.56 baseline with width, compute is the lever.

The 'sustainable replacements' framing is the plan's own, not asserted by the source.

items.page_quote: Our approach improved Hit@1 accuracy on ingredient substitution tasks, from the baseline 34.53 ± 0.10% to 38.03 ± 0.28% on the original GISMo dataset, and from 40.24 ± 0.36% to 54.46 ± 0.29% on a refined version of the same dataset.
items.note: The quote supports the direction (a larger/LLM model raises Hit@1 vs baseline), but the specific mechanism 'larger encoders capture finer ingredient context' is not stated anywhere on the page, so that part of the hypothesis is unsupported.

The prediction (Hit@1 rising with width) needs no source, but it embeds a factual claim 'GISMo's Hit@1 = 20.56' with no cited source in this item. GISMo Table 1 does report 20.56±0.14, so the number is accurate, but the item cites no source for it.

The prediction (plateau near GISMo's baseline) needs no source, but it embeds a factual claim 'GISMo's Hit@1 = 20.56' with no cited source. Table 1 does state 20.56±0.14, but this item cites no source.

The method/plan (reproduce, train at four widths/seeds) is what the plan will build/measure and needs no source, but it references 'GISMo's Recipe1MSubs result' and 'the 20.56 baseline' as facts with no cited source. The 20.56 number does appear in Table 1.

items.page_quote: We fine-tuned models, including OpenAI's GPT-3.5, DaVinci, and Meta's TinyLlama, using an ingredient substitution dataset. ... Our approach improved Hit@1 accuracy on ingredient substitution tasks, from the baseline 34.53 ± 0.10% to 38.03 ± 0.28% on the original GISMo dataset ...
items.note: Page confirms first author Luis Rita (2024), fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 and TinyLlama (also DaVinci), and Hit@1 lift from 34.53 to 38.03 on the GISMo dataset (Recipe1MSubs). The 'no capacity sweep within one protocol exists' clause is the plan's inference, not stated on the page, but the cited factual claims are all supported.

'The only scaling evidence is cross-protocol' is a factual claim about the state of the literature with no cited source; it cannot be verified from the fetched pages (the Rita abstract shows one cross-protocol LLM improvement, and neither page demonstrates a within-protocol capacity sweep, but 'only' cannot be established from these two pages).
Table 1 gives GISMo test-set MRR 31.51 and Hit@1 20.56, matching the anchor and its value 31.51; the paper also states the official code is available (github.com/facebookresearch/gismo).

The factual claims ('home recipes, not industrial formulations' and 'never measures environmental footprint or sensory quality') have no cited source in this item. They are consistent with the GISMo paper (Recipe1M home recipes; MRR/Hit@k ranking metrics only), but the item cites no source.
